title: Scientists say asteroid Bennu holds material that may have helped build Earth
byline: Cult of MacFollowAnkita SharmaTue, September 29, 2026 at 1:17 AM UTCAdd us on Google
excerpt: Samples from the asteroid Bennu reveal clues about the material that may have helped build other asteroids and rocky planets and sheds light on how Jupiter might a part of this process.
content:
Scientists studying samples from asteroid Bennu say the space rock preserves a chemical mix that is close to the raw material that built the terrestrial planets, including Earth. These findings were published in the Science Advances journal on September 23.

A team of scientists at ETH Zurich in Switzerland, led by isotope geochemist Maria Schönbächler, analyzed a piece of the material delivered to Earth by NASA's OSIRIS-REx spacecraft in 2023.

These findings challenge previous ideas about the origins of asteroid Bennu. Researchers had assumed asteroids like Bennu formed in the cold outer solar system, possibly near where comets were born.

The ETH team instead argues that Bennu's parent body took shape about 4.5 billion years ago near the water ice line, the boundary where water vapor freezes into ice. Bennu itself is a rubble pile made from the fragments of that larger body.

Bennu shares its fingerprint with Ryugu

Schönbächler's lab received about half a gram of Bennu's material sample, a fraction of the 121.6-gram sample parachuted to Earth in 2020. The capsule containing the sample landed in the Utah desert on September 24, 2023. It is the largest asteroid sample ever gathered in space.

The team of scientists measured the isotopes of iron, titanium, and chromium. Isotopes are versions of the same element with slightly different masses, and they together work like a fingerprint that can give hints about where the rock was originally formed.

Iron and titanium were spread evenly throughout Bennu. Chromium varied slightly between portions of the sample, which scientists report likely reflects water altering the parent body.

This composition pattern also matches the asteroid Ryugu. Japan's Hayabusa2 mission had previously obtained a sample of a little over 5 grams from this asteroid. Both asteroids have isotopic composition similar to a rare class of carbon-rich meteorites called CI chondrites.

This similarity suggests Bennu, Ryugu, and CI chondrites formed from a common dust reservoir.

How Jupiter and the ice line helped shape Bennu's parent asteroid

The scientists hypothesized that Jupiter played a central role in shaping the body of Bennu's parent asteroid. They estimated that the giant planet was formed within about a million years of the birth of our Sun.

As the giant planet grew, it blocked coarse materials from drifting inward, while fine dust from different regions of the disk flowed around it and mixed thoroughly near the ice line. The ice helped bind the tiny grains into the parent bodies of Bennu and its cousins.

This would explain why Bennu is rich in water and why its makeup is so uniform. It also suggests that Bennu contains material from both the inner and outer solar system. In ETH's official announcement, Schönbächler called Bennu a hybrid.

What Bennu can tell us about Earth's building blocks

Since the fine dust particles mixed so well, Bennu's composition can be said to resemble that of the Sun's. Schönbächler says this makes Bennu one of the best available views of the original mix of elements behind rocky planets.

ETH also adds that this describes the ingredients and not proof that Bennu's own material ended up inside Earth. The university also says that the asteroid's water and organic content offer clues about how the young Earth acquired the building blocks of life.

However, questions remain. The team of scientists still does not know whether other asteroids share the same signature as Bennu and Ryugu, or how much the young Jupiter helped shape the fine-dust mix.

In other news, China's Tianwen-2 reached the near-Earth asteroid Kamo'oalewa in July and is expected to return its samples in November 2027. Japan's Martian Moons eXploration mission is also scheduled to launch in October, with plans to return material samples from Mars' moon Phobos in 2031.

Scientists are still debating whether Phobos is a captured asteroid or formed from debris blasted off Mars. Further analysis is required, for which more samples are needed. Schönbächler told ETH she plans to apply to Japan's space agency for a share of sample material.
